title: Argument mapping and steelmanning
note: An argument map lays out the main conclusion, the reasons for it, and the objections, with arrows showing support. Linked premises support the conclusion only together; convergent premises each support it alone. Before you criticize, apply the principle of charity: reconstruct the argument in its strongest reasonable form, then test that version.

src.t: Informal Logic, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Sec. 3)

read.title: Map it, then make it strong
text: Long arguments are hard to judge in prose. An argument map helps by putting the main conclusion at the top and the reasons beneath, with arrows showing which claims support which. Objections hang off the claims they attack.

Maps reveal structure. Some premises are linked: 'all metals conduct electricity' and 'copper is a metal' support 'copper conducts' only together, so if either fails, that line of support collapses. Other premises are convergent: three independent witnesses each give a separate reason to think the suspect was there, so losing one leaves the others standing.

Before mapping someone else's argument, apply the principle of charity. Fill unstated gaps with the most plausible premise that would make the reasoning work, not the silliest. Steelmanning goes further: state the opposing view in the strongest form you can, ideally so well that its defenders would say you put it better than they did. Then criticize.

This is not mere politeness. If you refute only a weak version, the strong version is still standing, and you have learned nothing. If the strong version survives your best objection, you have learned something too.

q.q: Why are the copper premises called linked?
o: They support the conclusion only together

q.q: According to the reading, what happens if you refute only a weak version of a view?
o: The strong version is still standing

q.q: What does charity recommend for unstated gaps?
o: Fill them with the silliest premise
Fill them with the most plausible premise that makes it work
